You say what you like and dislike, talk about hobbies, and agree or disagree with others.
What do you like doing in your free time?
To use GUSTAR with every person: me, te, le, nos, os, les.
To say what you love (encantar) and what you can’t stand.
To agree: “a mí también / a mí tampoco”, or disagree: “a mí sí / a mí no”.
To talk about sports and hobbies: jugar, tocar, preferir.
What are you doing at the weekend?
After class, Mihai, Ana and Kenji have a coffee and talk about what they like.
Kenji, what do you like doing in your free time?
I love cooking. And I really like reading.
I like reading too! What about sports?
I don’t like them very much. I prefer swimming: I go to the pool on Saturdays.
Well, I love football. I play with some friends on Sundays.
I don’t like football at all. It’s so boring!
Boring? Impossible! And what do you like, Ana?
I love music and dancing. I play the guitar and dance flamenco.
Flamenco? How interesting! I really like Spanish music.
I don’t like dancing. I’m a terrible dancer.
Me neither. But I like watching!
Then on Friday there’s a flamenco show. Are you coming?
Of course! And on Sunday, everyone to the football.
Fine… OK. But just this once.
In GUI and GUE, the u is silent: guitarra = “gee-ta-rra”, with a hard g as in “get”.
Película, música, espectáculo: the stress falls on the third-to-last syllable, which is why they have a written accent.
Juego = “hweh-go”: a harsh j + the diphthong ue in a single syllable.
You’ve already learned “me gusta” = “I like”. Think of it literally as “it pleases me”: the thing you like is the subject, and the person is “to me, to you, to him…”.
The verb changes according to what is liked, not who likes it: one thing → gusta; several things → gustan; an action (infinitive) → gusta.
Wrong: “Yo gusto el fútbol” (that would mean “I am pleasing to football”). Correct: “Me gusta el fútbol” = “football pleases me”.
2. “A mí”, “a ti”, “a Ana”: for clarity or emphasis
You can double the person for emphasis or clarity:
I like tea, but you like coffee.
“Le gusta” can mean “he / she likes” or “you (polite) like”. You add “a + the person” to make it clear: a Mihai le gusta…
“Encantar” works just like “gustar”, but it’s stronger: “I love”.
I don’t like it at all 😖
With “encantar” you don’t add “mucho” or “muy”: “me encanta”, not “me encanta mucho”. It’s already the maximum.
4. Do you agree? también / tampoco / sí / no
The short answers depend on what the other person said, positive or negative:
After a negative sentence, “me neither” is “a mí TAMPOCO”, not “también” — just like English “me neither”, not “me too”.
With ordinary verbs (not gustar) you use “yo”: “Trabajo mucho. — Yo también.” / “No fumo. — Yo tampoco.”
English uses “play” for both games and instruments. Spanish doesn’t: JUGAR (a + sport) for games, TOCAR for instruments.
I play football / tennis. (al = a + el)
I play the piano / the guitar.
“Jugar la guitarra” is wrong. For instruments always use TOCAR.
I don’t like football at all.
¿Qué hacen los españoles en su tiempo libre?
A short article about free time in Spain.
Spaniards love being out and about.
In the evening many people go out for a walk or for a drink with friends.
Going “de tapas” is one of their favourite activities: it means eating small dishes in several bars.
The most popular sport is football. Many families watch matches together on Sundays.
But not everyone likes football: basketball and tennis are very popular too.
Young people really like music. In summer there are lots of festivals.
Older people prefer walking in the park or playing cards.
Reading isn’t the Spaniards’ favourite activity, but libraries have more and more visitors.
At the weekend, many families like to go to the countryside or the beach.
And in the evening… Spaniards love having dinner late and talking a lot!

Every Saturday morning, a group of friends meets in a café in Lavapiés. They call it “the Saturday club”.
They are very different people, but they all love talking about their passions.
Kenji likes cooking and really likes baseball. He always brings something to eat for the group.
Lena loves music. She plays the guitar and sings in a choir on Wednesdays.
Tom prefers sport: he runs every day and plays tennis at the weekend.
He doesn’t like reading at all. “Books bore me,” he always says.
Ana, on the other hand, absolutely loves books. She reads two or three novels a month.
Mihai is the calmest. He likes walking in the mountains and photographing birds.
He also likes football, like Tom. They both support Real Madrid… or so they say.
This Saturday they have a problem: they want to do an activity together, but they can’t agree.
Tom wants to go running. Lena prefers a concert. Ana wants to go to a bookshop, and Kenji to a market.
In the end Mihai has an idea: “What if we go on a trip to the mountains? We can walk, take photos, eat Kenji’s food and sing with Lena’s guitar.”
“And the books?”, asks Ana. “You can read on the train,” answers Mihai. Everyone thinks it’s perfect.
